## Problem

A release artefact sits on the lab disk. It may be a Kailash ISO or
qcow2, or any software the lab is about to run. "It downloaded" is
not a claim the assessment can stand behind. Before it boots, three
provably-checked statements matter. WHAT is inside it (an SBOM).
WHERE/HOW it was built (signed provenance). The bytes on disk are the
bytes the project shipped (the whole-file identity check). Kailash
ships the D-4 tooling; it makes every statement possible.

## Solution

Two chains exist: verify a Kailash release artefact against its
published records. Generate SBOM/provenance evidence for host-owned
artefacts. Both start the same way — identity first:

```bash
# ---------- CHAIN A: a downloaded kailash release artefact ----------
# 1. Whole-file identity (THE authority — the release's SHA256SUMS sheet)
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

# 2. Signed build provenance (SLSA v1.0 predicate; + the SPDX SBOM
#    attestation the pipeline recorded per artefact)
gh attestation verify kailash-<tag>-kailash-iso-<target>.iso \
    -R kailash-os/kailash-os
#    -> PASS requires: valid Sigstore signature chain, the repo's OIDC
#       identity, predicate https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1

# 3. The signed release tag
git tag -v <tag>

# 4. Inspect what the provenance itself contains (offline read)
gh attestation download kailash-<tag>-kailash-iso-<target>.iso -R kailash-os/kailash-os
jq . sha256:<digest>.jsonl | head    # the in-toto statement + predicate

# ---------- CHAIN B: make the same evidence for your own artefact ----
# 5. Generate an SBOM of the artefact/dir, in a standard format
syft <image-or-dir> -o cyclonedx-json=<art>.cdx.json
syft <image-or-dir> -o spdx-json=<art>.spdx.json

# 6. Validate + convert the SBOM with the CycloneDX CLI (validation is
#    the step that makes the document citable, not just creatable)
cyclonedx-cli validate --input-file <art>.cdx.json --input-format json

# 7. Vulnerability-check the SAME artefact off the SBOM you just made
grype sbom:<art>.cdx.json

# 8. AI-flavoured surfaces: an AI-BOM for model/prompt/MCP content
cdxgen -o aibom.json --profile <profile> .    # or the aibom flow per --help

# 9. Record what moved between two builds of the same artefact
cyclonedx-cli diff <old>.cdx.json <new>.cdx.json
```

Expected output shape (abridged):

```
$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-iso-full.iso: OK
$ gh attestation verify kailash-2026.01-alpha.1-kailash-iso-full.iso \
     -R kailash-os/kailash-os
Verified against repository kailash-os/kailash-os
... predicateType: https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 ...
$ grype sbom:art.cdx.json
<vulnerability table — or the "no vulnerabilities" shape>
```

What success looks like:

- every chain-A step passes: OK digest, attestation verified over the
  repo identity, and a good tag signature
- the generated SBOM parses clean under `cyclonedx-cli validate`
- grype's verdict runs against the host's OWN generated SBOM
  (provenance from evidence, not from trust)
- the host's `syft`/`cdxgen` documents record tool versions in their
  metadata. Name them when citing the SBOM

## Discussion

- **The three statements are deliberately separate records.** The
  SHA256SUMS sheet is artefact-identity (was this the shipped
  file?). The attestation is build-provenance (from what repo
  revision, in what workflow, with a Sigstore-signed SLSA v1.0
  predicate). Kailash's KA-48 slice attaches one per published
  artefact alongside the SPDX SBOM. The SBOM is content (what
  packages/components are inside). Any one alone leaves a gap: a
  digest without provenance is an unsigned claim. Provenance without
  an SBOM says nothing about what is IN the thing.
- **Standards, nameable precisely:** provenance predicates are
  in-toto attestations of type `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1`
  (SLSA v1.0's
  build-provenance statement). Verification follows GitHub's
  `gh attestation verify` contract, with JSONL export for offline/OIG
  review. SBOMs come in two dialects here: CycloneDX (JSON) and SPDX
  (JSON). `cyclonedx-cli`
  validates/diffs/merges CycloneDX, and the AI-BOM rides it. NIST-style
  minimum-elements compliance usually names SPDX/NTIA. `syft` and
  `cdxgen` both emit either dialect. Kailash's own release SBOM
  attestation is the SPDX one. Downstream evidence gathering should
  generate BOTH and cite each where it fits.
- **Why grype over the SBOM and not over the image:** scanning the
  generated SBOM keeps the evidence chain in one place — the document
  the run is about to file is the document that was scanned. (grype
  happily takes images too; the sbom: route makes the record
  reproducible.)
- **Nix caveat that shapes the SBOM's meaning:** a NixOS closure's
  packages are store paths, not a runtime filesystem tree. SBOM
  statements about a kailash image are statements about a declared
  closure. So the flake lock itself is the authoritative
  "what tools" record, and the SBOM is the portable, standard
  rendering of it for consumers outside Nix. Both views describe the
  same build; keep them in one story.
- **Where this rides in the project's own gates:** the release-cut
  checklist records `gh attestation verify ... PASS` per shipped
  artefact on every cut — the maintainer practice and the recipe are
  the same command. The attestations are made BY the release pipeline
  (actions/attest, SLSA v1.0 + SPDX per artefact); this recipe makes
  the lab the able counterparty of those records.
- **Not a scanner substitute:** grype's verdicts are point-in-time
  vulnerability facts about the SBOM's components. Provenance proves
  the build. The SBOM proves the content. Grype proves no KNOWN CVE in
  that content today. Keep all three claims distinct when reporting.
